extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, literature, and creative writing interested in the history and critique of European thought and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Extractive evaluative guidance for judging and producing philosophical writing and poetry in the medieval-to-early-modern European tradition, emphasising dangers of empty scholasticism, the roles of mysticism and national character, and national poetic characteristics. Useful for literary-historical criticism and creative-writing informed by historical poetics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid empty ideas and meaningless words (scholasticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The prevalence of empty ideas and meaningless words is a malady incident to human reason..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat vacuous verbal systems as a substantive flaw. The text identifies scholasticism/Aristotelic word-systems as 'empty logical system[s] of words' that produce little genuine knowledge. Anti-patterns: privileging formulaic terminology, abstract nominal definitions divorced from lived truth. Scoring note: penalise writing that substitutes verbal subtlety for substantive insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake skillful form (sophistry) for truth
rubrics_metrics.description: "we do not allow ourselves to hold sophistry to be less dangerous, merely because it presents itself in a form of greater skill and elegance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate arguments and prose by their truth-content, not rhetorical polish. Elegant presentation can mask error; be suspicious of technically sophisticated but substantively empty works. Provide examples of sophistry to show how form can mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for pernicious influence of empty ideas in public life
rubrics_metrics.description: "its most pernicious influences are exerted in active life by means of the distorted artifices of eloquence..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing persuasive writing (political, polemical, public-facing literature), penalise the use of rhetorical distortion that produces social/ethical harm. The problem is worse in active affairs than in purely scholastic exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empty reasoning breeds sectarian spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: "In every case, however, the spirit of sect is its inevitable consequence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to discursive patterns that cultivate factionalism: conclusions framed as absolute dogma, rhetorical tactics designed to exclude alternative views. Value openness and universality over sect-making rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should be appropriately integrated with religious/moral conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: "The philosophy of the middle age may be said to have been defective, chiefly because it was not thoroughly Christian; because the intellect, knowledge, and ideas of mankind, were not sufficiently penetrated with the spirit of our religion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In contexts where religion or moral conviction is central to the intellectual tradition being assessed, judge whether philosophical work is sufficiently situated within that moral-religious horizon. (This is a normative claim in the text reflecting its historical frame; use cautiously and note historical contingency.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise the two dangerous tendencies: over-rationalism and visionary Platonism
rubrics_metrics.description: "On the one hand... over-rationalism to which men are led by Aristotle... the other is the Platonic and visionary system of error..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating philosophical systems or creative works, identify whether they err toward excessive rationalism (reducing phenomena to dry abstraction) or toward ungrounded visionary speculation (detaching from empirical or moral anchors). Both tendencies are seen as leading to distinct errors; balance is ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystic/Platonic thought: appropriate for religious feeling, not for scientific matters
rubrics_metrics.description: "So long as men confined themselves to the subjects of religious feeling and conscience, there is no doubt that this philosophy was not merely an excusable but a very excellent guide. But its defectiveness was very apparent when they attempted to apply it to matters of science."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit visionary, mystical, or symbolic modes within religious, poetic, or ethical writing, but mark them down when they are asserted as natural-scientific explanations. Anti-pattern: treating occult or metaphysical symbolism as empirical account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platonism plus oriental mysteries tends to fancy, astrology, and magic
rubrics_metrics.description: "Platonism, connected as it was with a host of oriental mysteries... gave the fancy too much room for play, and in natural science in particular, the adoption of its tenets was almost always coupled with a belief in astrology, and a leaning to the study of magic."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When historicizing or emulating Platonist-influenced work, account for its receptivity to speculative and esoteric elements; treat claims of occult causation or astrological determinism skeptically in scientific or practical genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep occult/secret studies in their proper (limited) place
rubrics_metrics.description: "I am not disposed to throw entire ridicule even upon the study of secret influences, when it is kept in its proper place. But the application of such pursuits to the business of active life... are absurdities..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occult or speculative motifs may be tolerated as literary or speculative devices, but condemn their transfer into guides for public decision-making or ethical governance. Evaluate genre-appropriateness of such material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish serious mystical philosophers from charlatans and quacks
rubrics_metrics.description: "All the dabblers in the occult sciences were not men of this kind; the facility with which such pursuits could be associated with the most profligate schemes of quackery and charlatanery is too apparent..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess authorship and method: prize careful, erudite, and sincere engagement with mystical ideas, and criticise opportunistic, fraudulent, or commercially exploitative occultism. Use biographical/contextual evidence to separate rigorous thinkers from charlatans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let personal follies wholly negate a thinker's merits
rubrics_metrics.description: "It would be as unjust as foolish to deny the merits of these great men... to call in question their genius, their knowledge, or their piety, on account of their addiction to follies..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating historical figures, separate substantive achievements (genius, learning, piety) from errors or follies in other domains. Contextualise mistakes rather than using them to wholly discredit other contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for national character shaping philosophy and poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the philosophy of the middle age, as in that of the more modern times, the strong and distinct influence of national character is abundantly visible..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works in light of national temperaments and cultural tendencies (e.g., France/England favoring Aristotelic empiricism; Italy/Germany leaning toward Platonic mysticism). Use national-historical context as a criterion rather than treating works as culturally neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value restoration of ancient literature while weighing its revived errors
rubrics_metrics.description: "The renewed acquaintance with the literature of Greece had, on the whole, no other effect upon this mystical and more Platonic mode of philosophizing, but that of affording to it new materials... an influx of visionary opinions accompanied the change..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising revival movements, acknowledge both enrichment (new materials, instruments) and risks (revival of outdated or visionary errors). Balance advantages against introduced pathologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotle and Plato as enduring master-guides; other systems are by-paths
rubrics_metrics.description: "Plato and Aristotle have so distinctly marked out the two great paths of human thought and science, that they have remained... the master-guides of all succeeding generations. The other systems... are valuable... only because they resemble one or other of these."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In critical taxonomy, prioritise Aristotelian and Platonic frameworks as organizing principles. Other schools should be judged by their proximity or divergence from these main traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer internal, living change over merely external restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: "A restoration it undoubtedly was... But I can by no means approve of calling it a second birth of the human intellect... I should consider that name as due... to one which consists of an awakening out of previous death..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing movements (literary or intellectual), distinguish superficial/regulative restorations (external improvements) from deep transformative awakening (internal renewal). Reward genuine conceptual renewal over cosmetic revival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep poetry connected to philosophy; avoid their separation
rubrics_metrics.description: "We must always regard it as unlucky that they should spring up without any connection with philosophy, that the cultivation of the imagination should be separated from that of the understanding..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value works where imagination and intellect are integrated. Penalise art that divorces feeling from thought or vice versa; prefer poetry that engages philosophically and philosophy that retains poetic sensibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware that exclusively popular (vulgar) poetry signals cultural decline
rubrics_metrics.description: "The very existence of a poetry of the vulgar is in itself a sufficient evidence of the decline and corruption of true poetry; for that is a possession which should not belong peculiarly either to the common people or to the learned, but equally to all..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically view the rise of a mass/popular poetry that displaces a shared, national poetic culture—see it as possibly symptomatic of cultural imbalance. However, treat this as a historically situated claim rather than universal law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius and true philosophy are not the privilege of erudition
rubrics_metrics.description: "The gift of nature and God are open to all; the spirit of deep reflection... is by no means confined to the polished classes..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works and philosophers for originality and depth regardless of formal education or erudition. Prize internal inspiration and practical achievement over mere scholarly learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of old Castilian/Spanish poetry: strength, simplicity, and early absence of Arabic ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: "The old Castilian poems are... distinguished by a strength and simplicity both of language and of feeling, which bear the sure marks of a very different origin... the old Castilian poems are quite free from any such Arabian influence..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing historical Spanish/Castilian verse, expect and reward plain strength and simplicity in language and feeling; note absence of Arabic/Oriental ornament in the earliest strata and increasing Arabic influence in later works as a historical signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits of Spanish chivalric romances: polished writing, tender and idyllic representation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Their Chivalric Romances... are distinguished... by a more polished and beautiful mode of writing than is elsewhere to be found, and by a prevailing fondness for tender and idyllic representations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate chivalric romances for refinement of diction and a preference for idyllic/tender motifs; these are positive characteristics in the Spanish tradition per the text. Compare against other national traditions for contrasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social provenance of poets: Spanish poetry cultivated mainly by nobles and knights
rubrics_metrics.description: "In general, ever since its first commencement, the poetry of Spain has always been more cultivated by nobles and knights than by mere literati and authors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading medieval and early-modern Spanish poetry, note the frequent aristocratic authorship and how social class may shape themes (chivalry, courtly love). Use authorship background as an interpretive criterion.
